_notes: Non-rendered field: destination facts and seasonality findings only. The app ignores keys it does not know. Planning rationale and open questions are kept outside the repo.

ROUTING: Rome Fiumicino (FCO) in and out. Pescara (PSR) is closer to the Adriatic end but is poorly connected internationally. The return leg from Vasto to FCO is ~3h on the A25/A24 — the longest single drive of the trip, still inside the 4-6h cap.
ROUTING: Rome itself is skipped beyond the airport — the mountains start 90 minutes east. Easy to add 2 nights in Rome at the end if wanted, since the route already returns there.

SEASONALITY (re-verified 30 Aug 2026): no alpine-resort shutdown pattern here — these are working hill towns, not ski resorts. BUT the Gran Sasso cable car is a real question mark. It reopened 15 June 2026 after cable replacement, and historically it takes its ordinary autumn maintenance break starting around 11 September — which would put it shut for an October visit. No 2026 autumn schedule was published as of 30 Aug. Ring Centro Turistico Gran Sasso (+39 0862 606143) before counting on it. Campo Imperatore is reachable by car on the SS17bis regardless, until the first real snow in November.

SEASONALITY: the high mountain roads (Campo Imperatore, Passo Godi, Passo San Leonardo, Blockhaus) are open in October but close on snow, typically from November. An early-October trip is comfortably clear; check ANAS before driving the highest ones.
TRAILS: hikes are chosen in the 8-12 km moderate range. Corno Grande's summit routes are exposed scrambles and are deliberately NOT in this itinerary.

PRACTICALITIES: this is the least-touristy destination in the collection. English is thin in the mountain interior and village supermarket hours are limited — Sulmona and Vasto are the reliable restock points.

CARD CAPTIONS — PRIMARY (migrated 2026-08-30): Gran Sasso & Campo Imperatore: Three nights based at Santo Stefano di Sessanio | Lago di Scanno & the Sagittario Gorge: Three nights at Sulmona, 40 minutes below the lake | The Majella: Three nights at Caramanico Terme, inside the park

CARD CAPTIONS — NATURE (migrated 2026-08-30): Campo Imperatore Plateau: Reachable by car on the SS17bis until the first snow, usually November | Gole del Sagittario: Slow driving — and an easy riverside trail at the base | Valle dell'Orfento, Majella: Free permit from the Caramanico visitor centre before you set off | Gole di Celano: About 11 km return; the walls narrow to a couple of metres | Abruzzo National Park & Civitella Alfedena: Dawn and dusk are when the wildlife is out

CARD CAPTIONS — CITIES (migrated 2026-08-30): Santo Stefano di Sessanio: Largely car-free — park below and walk in | Sulmona: Wednesday and Saturday market fills Piazza Garibaldi | Pacentro: Ten minutes from Sulmona — an hour is plenty | Vasto: Two nights at the end, on the Adriatic

CARD CAPTIONS — FOOD (migrated 2026-08-30): Arrosticini: Ordered by the dozen and eaten straight off the skewer | Confetti di Sulmona: Pelino has made them in Sulmona since 1783 | Maccheroni alla Chitarra: Cut on a wire frame called a chitarra — hence the name | Navelli Saffron: A gram costs less at source than a fraction of it does at home | Porchetta: Vans park at markets and motorway stops all the way to Rome

CARD CAPTIONS — THINGS TO DO (migrated 2026-08-30): The Gran Sasso Cable Car: Often shut for autumn maintenance from mid-September — ring ahead before relying on it | Grotte di Stiffe: Guided walk of about an hour; 10°C inside, bring a layer | The Navelli Saffron Harvest: The flowering lasts two or three weeks; farms sell direct at the roadside | Rocca Calascio at Sunset: Free and always open; go late for the light and the emptiness | Lunch on a Trabocco: Most close for the season in late October — book ahead
title: Wolves, Hill Towns & Arrosticini: Italy's Green Mountain Heart

ideaImage.caption: Rocca Calascio, the highest fortress in the Apennines

brief: Ninety minutes east of Rome and almost nobody goes. Three national parks stacked together, beech forests that turn gold in October, stone villages clinging to hillsides, a heart-shaped lake, and food that is all lamb, saffron, pasta and mountain cheese. Wilder and greener than northern Italy, at maybe a third of the crowds.

facts.bestSeason: October — beech forests in full colour, mountain roads still open, villages still awake
facts.language: Italian; very little English in the mountain interior
facts.timezone: Central European Time (UTC+2 until 25 October, then UTC+1)
facts.driving: Right-hand traffic, good motorways, narrow but well-surfaced mountain roads

primary.heading: The mountains nobody flies in for
primary.intro: Ninety minutes east of Rome: three national parks stacked against each other, a high plateau, and stone villages that have been where they are for a thousand years.

nature.heading: Beech forest, gorges and a high plateau
nature.intro: The greenest part of central Italy and easily the wildest — bears and wolves still live here, and the beech woods turn gold right through October.

cities.heading: Stone villages and one proper town
cities.intro: Most of these are hilltop hamlets you can cross in ten minutes. Sulmona is the exception: a real market town with a Roman aqueduct running down one side of the square.

food.heading: Lamb, saffron and sugared almonds
food.intro: Mountain cooking, done plainly. Skewered lamb by the dozen, pasta cut on a guitar-string frame, sheep's cheese, and the world's most expensive spice grown on the plateau above.

why.heading: Why go east instead of north
why.intro: Same country, a third of the crowds, and a landscape that is genuinely forested rather than farmed.

thingsToDo.heading: Cable cars, caves and saffron
thingsToDo.intro: Small, specific things you can do on the day you feel like it — a cable car to a plateau, a river inside a mountain, a purple field being picked by hand.

itinerary.description: Land in the evening, sleep by the airport, and skip the city entirely in the morning.
A restored stone village as a base, the vast Campo Imperatore plateau above it, and the ruined fortress at Rocca Calascio on the skyline.
A handsome market town with a Roman aqueduct down one side, a gorge drive up to a heart-shaped lake, and wolves and bears in the park beyond.
Deep beech forest, a river gorge you walk right into, hermitages cut into cliffs, and the best hiking of the trip.
Down to the Adriatic for two easy days — fishing piers on stilts, a coastal cycle path on an old railway, and Vasto's old town.
Three hours back across the peninsula on the A25, and home.

primaryHighlights.title: Gran Sasso & Campo Imperatore
primaryHighlights.description: Italy's "Little Tibet" — a 20 km high plateau under the tallest peak in the Apennines, with stone villages and a fortress on its edge.
primaryHighlights.caption: Corno Grande above Campo Imperatore

primaryHighlights.title: Lago di Scanno & the Sagittario Gorge
primaryHighlights.description: A heart-shaped mountain lake at the end of a genuinely spectacular gorge road — one of the best short drives in Italy.
primaryHighlights.caption: Heart-shaped Lago di Scanno from above

primaryHighlights.title: The Majella
primaryHighlights.description: The greenest, quietest national park in central Italy — beech forest, river gorges and hermitages carved into rock walls.
primaryHighlights.caption: Snow-capped Majella seen from the hills

natureHighlights.title: Campo Imperatore Plateau
natureHighlights.description: An enormous grassland plateau at 1,800 m with horses grazing on it — easy, flat walking with huge views in every direction.
natureHighlights.caption: Snow patches on Campo Imperatore's slopes

natureHighlights.title: Gole del Sagittario
natureHighlights.description: A limestone gorge so tight the road has to tunnel through it, with a river running at the bottom.
natureHighlights.caption: Road along the Sagittario gorge lake

natureHighlights.title: Valle dell'Orfento, Majella
natureHighlights.description: The signature Majella walk — around 10 km through beech woods, following a clear river the whole way.
natureHighlights.caption: The Orfento river inside its gorge

natureHighlights.title: Gole di Celano
natureHighlights.description: A slot canyon you walk straight up the middle of, with the rock closing in overhead.
natureHighlights.caption: Narrow limestone gorge entrance

natureHighlights.title: Abruzzo National Park & Civitella Alfedena
natureHighlights.description: Europe's best chance of seeing wild wolves and Marsican bears, in the oldest and most forested park in the region.
natureHighlights.caption: Civitella Alfedena beneath the mountain

cityHighlights.title: Santo Stefano di Sessanio
cityHighlights.description: A tiny medieval stone village at 1,250 m, carefully restored and very quiet.
cityHighlights.caption: Santo Stefano di Sessanio from below

cityHighlights.title: Sulmona
cityHighlights.description: The one proper town in the mountains — a long arcaded square, a Roman aqueduct, real shops, and the sugared-almond capital of Italy.
cityHighlights.caption: Piazza Garibaldi and the mountains behind

cityHighlights.title: Pacentro
cityHighlights.description: Three castle towers standing over a tight cluster of stone houses — the postcard Abruzzese village.
cityHighlights.caption: Church and fountain in Pacentro's piazza

cityHighlights.title: Vasto
cityHighlights.description: A bright old town on a bluff over the Adriatic — the relaxed, warm finish to a mountain trip.
cityHighlights.caption: Vasto's hillside skyline from the coast

culinaryHighlights.title: Arrosticini
culinaryHighlights.description: Skewers of mountain lamb grilled over a long, narrow charcoal trough built for nothing else.
culinaryHighlights.caption: Raw lamb skewers ready for grilling

culinaryHighlights.title: Confetti di Sulmona
culinaryHighlights.description: Sugared almonds built into enormous flower bouquets, which is how the whole town sells them.
culinaryHighlights.caption: Sugared-almond flower bouquets on display

culinaryHighlights.title: Maccheroni alla Chitarra
culinaryHighlights.description: Square-cut pasta pressed through a guitar-string frame, served with lamb ragù. Local, cheap, everywhere.
culinaryHighlights.caption: Pasta with tomato and small meatballs

culinaryHighlights.title: Navelli Saffron
culinaryHighlights.description: The most expensive spice in the world, grown on the plateau above L'Aquila and sold in tiny glass jars at the farm gate.
culinaryHighlights.caption: Farmer walking through the saffron fields

culinaryHighlights.title: Porchetta
culinaryHighlights.description: A whole pig boned, rolled with herbs and roasted overnight, then sliced into a bread roll from a van at the roadside. Central Italy's great street food.
culinaryHighlights.caption: Whole porchetta roast on a board

culinaryHighlights.title: Roman Pizza
culinaryHighlights.description: Square pizza with many different toppings, sold by weight.
culinaryHighlights.caption: Pizzeria counter in Rome

thingsToDo.title: The Gran Sasso Cable Car
thingsToDo.description: Italy's oldest working cable car, built in 1934, lifting you 1,000 m from Fonte Cerreto onto the Campo Imperatore plateau in ten minutes.
thingsToDo.caption: Road across the Campo Imperatore plateau

thingsToDo.title: Grotte di Stiffe
thingsToDo.description: A cave system with a river still running through it — waterfalls, rapids and a lake, all underground, on a lit walkway.
thingsToDo.caption: Stalagmites inside Grotte di Stiffe

thingsToDo.title: The Navelli Saffron Harvest
thingsToDo.description: Late October is when the purple crocus fields above L'Aquila are picked, entirely by hand, at dawn.
thingsToDo.caption: A saffron crocus in close-up

thingsToDo.title: Rocca Calascio at Sunset
thingsToDo.description: A twenty-minute walk up to a ruined fortress on a bare ridge at 1,460 m, with the whole Gran Sasso behind it.
thingsToDo.caption: Rocca Calascio's towers at dusk

thingsToDo.title: Lunch on a Trabocco
thingsToDo.description: Eating on a wooden fishing pier built out over the Adriatic on stilts, with the water moving under the floorboards.
thingsToDo.caption: A trabocco pier over the sea

otherPerks: Arrosticini come by the dozen off a charcoal trough and cost almost nothing
Wolves and brown bears still live here — Civitella Alfedena is where to look
Saffron grows on the plateau, and sells at source for a fraction of the usual
Beech forests turn gold through October while the mountain roads stay open
Restaurant bills run about a third of what Tuscany charges
The Adriatic stays warm enough to swim into mid-October
No crowds and no tour buses at all
Ninety minutes from a major airport to genuine wilderness
